html:
A requirement describes what the business needs; the data model is where that need becomes records, fields, and relationships. This phase teaches you to turn business nouns into objects and attributes into fields, choose Lookup versus Master-Detail relationships, write a data dictionary, and design a model that survives reporting needs — the bridge the CBA exam assumes between Requirements Elicitation and the platform-heavy phases that follow.

Learning Objectives

  • Map business nouns to objects and attributes to fields...
  • Choose Lookup vs Master-Detail relationships and justify the choice...
  • Design one-to-many and many-to-many models with and without junction objects...
  • Understand picklists, formula fields, and roll-up summaries...
  • Read and create a data dictionary entry for any field...
  • Distinguish standard objects from custom objects in a domain model...
  • Design a model that answers the reports asked of it...
  • Build and query the User_Story__c model with test classes and practice SOQL...

1. Why a BA Needs to Talk Data

The BA who cannot read a data model cannot finish a conversation. When a developer says "I'll make the sessions object a master-detail to Tutor," they have made a business decision in a language the business never approved. The BA who understands the model stays in the conversation: they ask whether a Tutor can exist without a Session, and the answer resolves an actual business rule. Data modeling is requirement work expressed in objects.

Two worlds supply the models. BrightLogistics provides the professional context — standard objects plus the BA's own working artifacts. StudyBuddy Tutoring is the domain-modeling playground: a tutoring agency with Students, Tutors, Sessions (one session equals one student plus one tutor), Session-Feedback, and Payments. Both stress the same skills: identifying what exists independently, what belongs to what, and what the model must let reports see.

2. From Business Nouns to Objects

Every object starts as a business noun — a thing with its own identity. Requirements become Business_Requirement__c; stories become User_Story__c; stakeholders Stakeholder__c; test cases UAT_Test_Case__c; a student becomes Student; a tutoring session becomes Session. The noun test: if "a {noun} exists" makes sense alone, it qualifies.

Business nounObjectAttributes to fields
RequirementBusiness_Requirement__cType, Priority, Status, Value
User storyUser_Story__cPoints, Status, Acceptance
StakeholderStakeholder__cRACI, Influence, Interest
Test caseUAT_Test_Case__cStep, Expected, Actual, Status
Tutoring session (StudyBuddy)SessionDate, Tutor, Student, Duration

The rule that keeps a model healthy: if two things can exist independently, model them as separate objects and relate them — do not cram nouns into one object because they "feel related." A Test Case and its Steps are different granularities; a Requirement and its Stakeholder are different identities. Cramming produces the mega-object whose fields are half-empty and whose reports are tortured.

3. Attributes to Fields

Once the noun is an object, its characteristics become fields. An attribute is anything you can state about the object on a form or report: a status, a date, a score, an owner, a description. The type follows what the business will ask: a number for scores, a picklist for finite states, a date for chronology, a long text for narrative, a lookup for "which other record does this point back to."

The discipline is to let the reporting future vote on the field type. The User_Story__c model shows the pattern: Story_Points__c is a Number because the backlog is summed by points; Priority__c and Status__c are Picklists because their values are finite; Priority_Score__c is a Formula or Number because the backlog sorts by it. Ask what reports run on this field before locking the type — that question is worth more than any platform shortcut.

4. Standard Objects: The Shared CRM Domain

Salesforce ships standard objects for the common CRM domain: Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity, Case, Task, Event. A BA must know them well enough to catch when a standard object satisfies the requirement with zero custom metadata. At BrightLogistics the inbound web lead is a Lead, the freight client an Account with Contacts, the deal an Opportunity, and the tracking dashboard reads standard fields.

The trap is forcing a square peg into a standard object because it exists. A tutoring Session does not fit any standard object without gymnastic field abuse — that noun gets a custom object. The balance is the entire skill: standard objects accelerate the common (leads, cases, opportunities), custom objects handle the specific. The exam rewards naming the standard object for a common need and the custom object for a genuine gap.

5. Custom Objects and the StudyBuddy Domain

Custom objects carry the __c suffix and model nouns the platform does not know. In StudyBuddy, Students and Tutors are separate objects (they exist independently; a Tutor is not a field of a Student). A Session connects one student and one tutor, so Session holds two lookups. Session-Feedback belongs to a session and has no life without it — the classic child record. Payments are trickier: a family may pay per session or prepay a balance, so Payments relate to Sessions loosely.

The BA's job on the StudyBuddy model is deciding what each object owns and what it points to: Students own contact details and progress, Tutors own availability and rates, Sessions own pairing and time, Feedback owns evaluation, Payments own money. Each decision is a business rule fixed in advance.

6. Lookup vs Master-Detail Relationships

The relationship decision is the most exam-tested data modeling question, and it collapses to one business question: does the child have a life without the parent?

LookupMaster-Detail
Independent lifeBoth sides may exist aloneChild dies with the master
DeletesNo cascadeCascade delete
SharingFlexible, per recordChild inherits master's sharing
Roll-up summariesNot availableCOUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX
Relation fields per childUnlimitedMax two

Use Master-Detail when the child has no business meaning alone — test steps without their test case, feedback without its session. Use Lookup when the relationship is loose — a Payment that also exists as a prepayment balance. The constraint that drives the choice: roll-up summaries require Master-Detail, so the story record showing a count of its test cases makes test-case-to-story a Master-Detail.

7. Cardinality: One-to-Many and Many-to-Many

Cardinality is the mathematics of a relationship. One-to-many means one parent, many children — one Business_Requirement__c, many User_Story__c records. Many-to-many means records on both sides relate to many of each other; it never fits between two objects directly and needs a junction object holding two lookups.

StudyBuddy forces the junction decision. A Student attends many Sessions and a Tutor leads many, but each Session has exactly one of each — so Session itself is the junction carrying both lookups. Payments are genuinely many-to-many: a family can prepay a balance used across sessions, and one session may be paid by two family members, resolved through a Payment-Allocation junction with amount and session. Memory rule: two objects cannot hold a many-to-many directly; resolve through a junction.

8. Roll-Up Summary and Formula Fields

Roll-up summaries and formulas are where the model answers questions without code. A roll-up on the parent counts, sums, mins, or maxes its children — test cases per story, session time per tutor. Formulas compute from fields on the same record — a value/effort score, a gap score, an age in days. The BA specifies both while writing requirements; the platform does the arithmetic.

The constraint from section 6: roll-ups require Master-Detail. "Show total sessions per tutor" forces tutor-to-session to be Master-Detail — why StudyBuddy's Session design is a negotiation, not a default. Formulas need only fields: Value_Score__c times the inverse of Gap_Score__c is how the Backlog_Prioritization_Scoring Flow produces the number Phase 6 sorts on.

9. Picklists, Field Types, and Validation

The field types a BA chooses carry business meaning. A picklist is a controlled vocabulary — Status, Priority, RACI, severity — and controlling it is governance: users cannot type "n/a" if no such value exists, and reports stay clean by construction. Numbers carry ranges that must be validated (a Value_Score of 150 is impossible when a rule enforces 1-100); dates need business calendars, not formats.

Validation rules are the enforcement layer the BA writes in requirement language: score bounds, required-before-approval rules (the Acceptance_Criteria__c gate from Phase 4), date sanity. Five rules ship in the lab — score bounds, status transitions, answer formats. The BA writes the rule's intent; the platform makes it unbreakable.

10. The Data Dictionary

A data dictionary defines every object and field — type, picklist values, default, required flag, meaning — and it is the BA's contract with the build team. It is the legend to the model's map: without it, "Status" and "Status__c" drift apart until two teams mean different things. BrightLogistics' Business_Requirement__c dictionary lives in the metadata; StudyBuddy's would be written exactly this way:

FieldTypeValues / defaultRules
Status__cPicklistDraft, In Review, Approved, Implemented, Verified, RejectedRequired; default Draft
Priority__cPicklistMust Have / Should / Could / Won'tRequired
Value_Score__cNumber (1-100)—1-100 range validation
Acceptance_Criteria__cLong Text—Required before Approved

Read the dictionary like a contract: "Required before Approved" is enforced by validation; "default Draft" is honored at record creation. When the requirement set and the dictionary disagree, the dictionary is the working document — the BA reconciles them before the build.

11. Fields That Need Care: Required, Default, Unique

Three field settings deserve BA attention because they silently shape data quality. Required fields are a promise: if Status is required but unwanted on the creation form, users will invent a value to get past the screen. Defaults are the quieter contract: a Status defaulting to Draft means every record enters the funnel in the right place. Uniqueness is the governance hammer: duplicate Leads suppressed on email plus company is a uniqueness rule wearing a dedupe costume.

Each setting is a documented decision, not a click. "Why is Status required?" must have an answer in the dictionary; "why dedupe on email and company but not name?" has an answer in the BrightLogistics duplicate-lead complaint log. The lab's validation rules, defaults, and BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest exercise these settings end-to-end, so you watch a validation error fire.

12. Designing for Reporting First

Design for reporting first: ask what reports run on this data before locking field types. A Phase 4 reporting requirement — "executives see dispatch cycle by source" — forces a dispatch timestamp and a source field to exist, be populated, and be comparable. A model that stores what reports need survives; one that stores what the form conveniently collected needs a reporting retrofit, and retrofits cost more than design.

The rule produces concrete checks. Summable: are numbers numeric, not text? Groupable: are dimensions picklists, not free text? Timely: do date fields capture the moment the KPI needs? Traceable: can every report row trace to a record a stakeholder recognizes? Run the checks against BrightLogistics and StudyBuddy before anything deploys; Phase 10 builds the report layer on these fields.

13. The Lab: BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest and Practice SOQL

The lab closes the loop with code you read, run, and extend. BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest walks the whole Phase 5 model end-to-end: it creates a User_Story__c with points, priority, status, and acceptance criteria, inserts it, and asserts the round-trip. Its sibling query in scripts/soql/requirements.soql shows the model answering real questions.

apex
// BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest exercises the model end-to-end
User_Story__c s = new User_Story__c(
  Name                   = 'As a rep, I can log a call in one click',
  Story_Points__c        = 3,
  Status__c              = 'Backlog',
  Acceptance_Criteria__c = 'Call logged under 5 seconds'
);
insert s;
System.assertEquals('Backlog', s.Status__c);

Run it with sf apex run test --class-names BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest --target-org myDevOrg and you have proven the model: inserted, read back, asserted. Then edit the filters in scripts/soql/requirements.soql and watch the metadata answer your questions. The definitions live under force-app/main/default/objects/User_Story__c/, and this object is the exact table Phase 6's backlog and Phase 12's UAT rows hang from.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 5.1: StudyBuddy Object Mapping

  1. List the StudyBuddy nouns: Student, Tutor, Session, Session-Feedback, Payment.
  2. For each, write whether it can exist independently, and list four attributes that become fields.
  3. Group the nouns into objects, noting which attributes are references to other objects (lookups).
  4. Present a noun-to-object table with a field sketch per object.

Expected result: a table of five objects with independent-existence notes and a field sketch each. What it proves: you find object boundaries before any relationship is drawn. Pairs with Exercise 5.1 StudyBuddy object mapping in Phase 15.

Exercise 5.2: Lookup vs Master-Detail Decisions on StudyBuddy

  1. For each pair — Session to Student, Session to Tutor, Session-Feedback to Session, Payment to Session — answer "does the child have a life without the parent?"
  2. Assign Lookup or Master-Detail and justify each in one sentence.
  3. For the Payment many-to-many, sketch the junction object that resolves it.
  4. Name two roll-ups you could now build and the relationship each requires.

Expected result: a decision table with justifications, a junction sketch, and two named roll-up candidates. What it proves: you decide relationships from business rules, not platform convenience. Pairs with Exercise 5.2 Lookup vs Master-Detail in Phase 15.

Exercise 5.3: Write a Data Dictionary Entry

  1. Pick User_Story__c fields: Story_Points__c, Priority__c, Status__c, Priority_Score__c.
  2. Write a dictionary row for each: type, values/default, required flag, business meaning.
  3. Compare your rows to the definitions in force-app/main/default/objects/User_Story__c/.
  4. Fix any mismatch and note why.

Expected result: a four-row dictionary matching the deployed metadata, plus a note per row. What it proves: you can write — and audit — the BA contract with the build team. Pairs with Exercise 5.3 Data dictionary in Phase 15.

Exercise 5.4: Report-First Model Cheat Test

  1. Take one BrightLogistics report goal: dispatch cycle time by source.
  2. List the fields that report needs (dispatch timestamp, source, owner) and where they live.
  3. Check each: numeric, picklist, date, and populated on the right records?
  4. Propose the field changes that make the report work without a rebuild.

Expected result: a gap list of three-plus fields with named types, plus a two-line change proposal. What it proves: reporting needs drive data model decisions, not the other way around.

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
ObjectA container for records modeled on a business noun, such as Student or Business_Requirement__c.
FieldA typed attribute of an object, such as a picklist, number, date, or formula.
Standard objectA built-in object such as Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity, or Case.
Custom objectAn org-defined object whose API name ends in __c.
Lookup relationshipA loose link where both records may exist independently.
Master-Detail relationshipA tight link where the child lives and dies with the master.
Roll-up summaryA parent field that counts, sums, mins, or maxes its children; requires Master-Detail.
Junction objectThe object resolving a many-to-many relationship between two other objects.
CardinalityHow many records of one side relate to records of the other (1:N, N:N).
PicklistA controlled vocabulary field with a fixed set of values.
Validation ruleMetadata that rejects records violating a stated business rule.
Data dictionaryThe field-by-field contract defining type, values, defaults, and meaning.

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can turn business nouns into objects and attributes into fields.
  • I can justify Lookup vs Master-Detail from the child's independent life.
  • I can resolve a many-to-many relationship with a junction object.
  • I can explain when a roll-up summary requires Master-Detail and use its four functions.
  • I can read and write a data dictionary row that matches deployed metadata.
  • I can name the standard object for a common CRM need and the custom object for a gap.
  • I can design a model that answers a stated reporting requirement.
  • I can run BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest and extend practice SOQL against the model.

Summary

You learned to find object boundaries through the noun test, assign attributes to typed fields, and place everything on standard or custom objects. You can now choose Lookup or Master-Detail from the child's independent life, resolve many-to-many with junctions, and wield roll-ups and formulas where the platform does the arithmetic. You wrote a data dictionary as the contract with the build team, designed the model reporting-first, and proved it with BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest and practice SOQL — the foundation Phase 6's backlog and Phase 10's dashboards will stand on.
